demographics: Most commonly recognized in infants and toddlers, but can present at any age when growth or weight gain is inadequate
More often identified in children living in poverty or food insecurity

risk_factors.text: Feeding difficulties such as poor latch, reflux or oral aversion
Young maternal age or low parental education

family_history: Genetic or metabolic disorder in a sibling

chief_complaints.text: He just isn't gaining weight like he should
She seems smaller than other kids her age
He doesn't seem hungry and is hard to feed
She spits up a lot after feeds

hpi.onset: Gradual, noticed over weeks to months by the caregiver or at a well-child visit
hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months by the time it is brought to medical attention
hpi.progression: Slow or absent weight gain, often with a fall in weight-for-age or weight-for-length percentiles; length and head circumference may be affected later
hpi.quality: Inadequate weight gain or weight loss relative to age
hpi.severity: Mild to severe depending on duration and degree of deficit

associated_symptoms.text: Vomiting or spitting up after feeds

pertinent_negatives: Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours

argues_against: Chronic productive cough with weight loss

atypical.how_it_differs: Older children may present with short stature, delayed puberty or poor school performance rather than weight faltering alone.
Infants may present with feeding aversion, poor suck, or failure to regain birth weight rather than a clear growth plateau.
In older adults failure to thrive presents as unintentional weight loss, functional decline and frailty rather than poor growth.

general.mild: Alert, interactive, well-appearing but small for age; no acute distress
general.moderate: Thin, less interactive than expected for age, easily fatigued during the exam
general.severe: Markedly wasted, lethargic or irritable, poor tone, sunken eyes
general.critical: Cachectic, apathetic or unresponsive, hypotonic, signs of dehydration or shock

findings.maneuver: Weigh the child on a calibrated scale and plot weight-for-age and weight-for-length on the WHO/CDC growth chart
findings.finding: Weight below the expected percentile for age, or a fall across two or more major percentile lines

findings.maneuver: Measure recumbent length (or standing height) and plot on the growth chart
findings.finding: Length or height below the expected percentile for age

findings.maneuver: Measure occipitofrontal head circumference and plot on the growth chart
findings.finding: Head circumference below the expected percentile for age

findings.maneuver: Inspect the child undressed and assess subcutaneous fat over the trunk and limbs
findings.finding: Loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle mass with a wasted appearance

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctivae, oral mucosa and palmar creases
Pinch the abdominal skin and release, and assess the mucous membranes
findings.finding: Decreased skin turgor with dry mucous membranes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyes and periorbital area
Observe and elicit age-appropriate milestones and tone
Assess tone by passive range of motion and traction response
Inspect the face, hands and feet for dysmorphic features
Palpate the abdomen for liver and spleen size
Auscultate the heart in all four positions
Inspect the skin and sclerae for jaundice

labs.caveat: Anemia is usually from iron or other nutrient deficiency; microcytic with low ferritin points to iron deficiency.
Low MCV suggests iron deficiency; high MCV suggests B12 or folate deficiency.
Thrombocytopenia raises concern for bone marrow disease or severe nutritional deficiency.
Hyponatremia can reflect poor intake, vomiting, diuretic use or SIADH.
Hypokalemia from vomiting or diarrhea; hyperkalemia suggests renal failure or adrenal disease.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis from diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis or inborn error of metabolism.
Elevated BUN with normal creatinine suggests dehydration or prerenal azotemia.
Rising creatinine suggests dehydration or intrinsic renal disease.
Hypoglycemia in a poorly feeding infant is an emergency and can suggest an inborn error of metabolism or endocrine disorder.
Hypocalcemia can accompany rickets or hypoparathyroidism; check ionized calcium if albumin is low.
Low albumin suggests chronic malnutrition, malabsorption or protein-losing enteropathy.
Low total protein supports malnutrition or malabsorption.
Elevation suggests hepatic or metabolic disease.
Elevation suggests hepatic or metabolic disease.
Elevated TSH with low free T4 confirms hypothyroidism, a treatable cause of poor growth.
Low free T4 with high TSH confirms primary hypothyroidism.
Low ferritin is the most specific marker of iron deficiency; ferritin rises with inflammation.
Low B12 suggests dietary deficiency or malabsorption.
Low folate suggests dietary deficiency or malabsorption.
Elevation suggests an inflammatory or infectious process.
Nonspecific; supports inflammation or infection.
Proteinuria suggests renal disease contributing to poor growth.
Ketones reflect poor intake or vomiting.
High specific gravity suggests dehydration.
Screen the caregiver, not the child; caregiver depression is a common contributor.

differential.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
differential.why_considered: Frequent spitting up and poor weight gain in an infant is one of the most common reasons for faltering growth

exam: Well-appearing infant with normal tone and development
imaging: Upper gastrointestinal series shows reflux without anatomic obstruction

differential.name: Cow's milk protein allergy
differential.why_considered: Poor weight gain with vomiting, diarrhea or blood in the stool in a formula-fed or breastfed infant

history: Symptoms begin after introduction of cow's milk formula
imaging: Normal anatomy on upper gastrointestinal series

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal bloating and poor weight gain in a child old enough to eat gluten

history: Diarrhea and bloating after gluten introduction
imaging: Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Poor linear growth with weight gain, constipation and developmental delay in an infant or young child
differential.trigger: Short stature with delayed bone age, constipation or developmental delay

labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
imaging: Delayed bone age on hand and wrist radiograph

differential.name: Congenital heart disease
differential.why_considered: Poor feeding, sweating with feeds and poor weight gain in an infant with a cardiac lesion
differential.trigger: Murmur, cyanosis, tachypnea or sweating during feeds

imaging: Echocardiogram shows structural defect with shunt or obstruction

differential.name: Non-accidental trauma
differential.why_considered: Failure to thrive with injuries, inconsistent history or delayed presentation
differential.trigger: Injuries inconsistent with the stated mechanism or developmental stage

history: Inconsistent or changing explanation for injuries
exam: Bruises in various stages of healing
imaging: Skeletal survey shows fractures of differing ages, including metaphyseal corner fractures

differential.name: Inborn error of metabolism
differential.why_considered: Poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy and failure to thrive in a neonate or young infant
differential.trigger: Lethargy, vomiting and metabolic acidosis after feeding

history: Family history of sibling death in infancy
imaging: Normal brain MRI or nonspecific findings

differential.name: Psychosocial failure to thrive
differential.why_considered: Poor weight gain without an organic cause, often with food insecurity or caregiver stress

exam: Child is interactive and gains weight when fed by staff

severity.mild: Weight below the expected percentile or crossing one major percentile line, with normal length and head circumference and no dehydration
severity.moderate: Weight and length below expected percentiles, mild wasting, and possible developmental delay but no dehydration or metabolic derangement
severity.severe: Marked wasting, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, hypoglycemia or significant developmental delay
severity.critical: Shock, severe dehydration, hypoglycemia, hypothermia or life-threatening infection in a cachectic infant

red_flags.meaning: Severe malnutrition, hypoglycemia or sepsis; needs immediate evaluation and treatment

red_flags.finding: Signs of dehydration such as sunken eyes, decreased skin turgor or dry mucous membranes
red_flags.meaning: Significant fluid deficit requiring urgent rehydration
Can indicate an inborn error of metabolism or severe malnutrition; treat immediately
Possible non-accidental trauma; requires a skeletal survey and child protective services involvement
Suggests anatomic obstruction such as malrotation or pyloric stenosis; needs urgent imaging

complications.name: Short stature
clues: Length or height below expected percentile

special_populations.differences: Failure to thrive often presents as poor feeding, poor latch or failure to regain birth weight; careful assessment of feeding technique and caregiver-infant interaction is essential.
Older children may present with short stature, delayed puberty or poor school performance rather than weight faltering alone.

Failure to thrive in older adults presents as unintentional weight loss, functional decline and frailty rather than poor growth; the workup focuses on chronic disease, depression and medication effects.

key_questions.question: Can you walk me through what and how much your child eats and drinks in a typical day, including how feeds are prepared?
key_questions.looking_for: Caloric intake below what is expected for age, over-diluted or incorrectly prepared formula, or a feeding schedule that is too infrequent

key_questions.question: How does feeding go — does your child latch or suck well, turn away, arch, cough or choke during feeds?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor latch or suck, oral aversion, arching or choking that points to a feeding or swallowing problem

key_questions.question: How many wet diapers and stools does your child have each day, and what do the stools look like?
key_questions.looking_for: Few wet diapers suggests inadequate intake; frequent, greasy or bloody stools suggests malabsorption or allergy

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the growth problem, and has your child's weight been dropping on the growth chart over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over weeks to months with a fall across percentile lines rather than a single low measurement

key_questions.question: Has your child had any vomiting, and if so, is it forceful or green-tinged?
key_questions.looking_for: Bilious or projectile vomiting suggests anatomic obstruction such as malrotation or pyloric stenosis

key_questions.question: Has your child had any fever, cough, diarrhea or frequent infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent or chronic illness that raises metabolic demand or causes malabsorption

key_questions.question: Is your child meeting milestones — smiling, sitting, walking, talking — at the expected ages?
key_questions.looking_for: Developmental delay or regression, which suggests a neurologic, metabolic or endocrine cause

key_questions.question: Does your child have any known medical conditions, or was he or she born early or small?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity, low birth weight, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease or other chronic illness

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have short stature, celiac disease, thyroid problems or a genetic or metabolic disorder?
key_questions.looking_for: Familial short stature, celiac disease, hypothyroidism or an inherited metabolic disorder

key_questions.question: Do you ever worry about having enough food for your family, or about paying for formula or food?
key_questions.looking_for: Food insecurity, which is a common and modifiable contributor to poor growth

key_questions.question: How are things going at home — who cares for your child, and how are you feeling yourself?
key_questions.looking_for: Caregiver depression, substance use, role strain or neglect that affects feeding and care

key_questions.question: Has your child been around any sources of lead, such as old paint or dust from a renovation?
key_questions.looking_for: Lead exposure, which can contribute to poor growth and developmental delay

reasoning_points: Serial weight, length and head circumference plotted on the correct WHO or CDC growth chart, showing a fall across percentile lines or weight below the expected percentile for age
A thorough feeding history including what, how much, how often and how the child feeds, since inadequate intake is the most common cause
Assessment of caregiver-child interaction and screening for food insecurity and caregiver depression

Growth pattern helps localize the cause: weight alone affected suggests inadequate intake, while weight and length affected suggests endocrine or systemic disease, and head circumference involvement suggests early or severe insult
Targeted laboratory testing for treatable causes such as anemia, hypothyroidism, renal disease and malabsorption rather than a broad untargeted panel
Red flags such as bilious or projectile vomiting, lethargy, hypoglycemia or injuries inconsistent with the history prompt urgent evaluation and imaging
Consideration of non-accidental trauma when injuries or an inconsistent history are present

easy: Infant with a clear fall in weight percentile and an obvious feeding problem such as over-diluted formula or an infrequent feeding schedule
Caregiver reports food insecurity and the child gains weight appropriately during hospitalization
Classic presentation with poor weight gain, normal length and head circumference, and no red flags
medium: Infant with frequent spitting up and irritability during feeds suggesting gastroesophageal reflux disease
Toddler with chronic diarrhea and bloating after gluten introduction suggesting celiac disease
Child with constipation, cold intolerance and delayed milestones suggesting hypothyroidism
Infant with a murmur and sweating during feeds suggesting congenital heart disease
hard: Neonate with poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy after feeds suggesting an inborn error of metabolism
Child with injuries in different stages of healing and an inconsistent history suggesting non-accidental trauma
Older child presenting with short stature and delayed puberty rather than weight faltering alone
Infant with failure to regain birth weight and a subtle feeding aversion without an obvious organic cause
